name: Carrageenan (iota-carrageenan nasal spray, sprayed into the nose)
short: Case report: anaphylaxis to carrageenan in a barium enema (rectal, not nasal). Nasal spray: adverse events like salt-water placebo in 200 adults, fewer in 153 children, similar in 42 pollen-allergic.
text: Apart from one allergy case report, these data concern carrageenan sprayed into the nose; none of the cited trials covers carrageenan eaten as a food additive. Allergy (a different route, a barium enema given rectally, not the nasal spray): a case report describes anaphylaxis during a barium enema in a patient with no latex exposure or latex allergy; carrageenan, a component of the enema solution, gave positive allergy skin tests and a positive RAST blood test for specific IgE antibodies, and the gut symptoms for which the patient was being investigated later disappeared on a carrageenan-free diet. The authors describe carrageenan as a previously unreported cause of anaphylaxis during barium enema and as an allergen widely distributed in common foods. The abstracts of the cited nasal-spray trials do not describe an allergic reaction to the spray. In a randomised, double-blind trial in 200 adults with early cold symptoms who used a 0.12% iota-carrageenan spray or a salt-water placebo spray four times daily for 4 to 10 days, treatments were well tolerated with no differences in adverse event rates. In a randomised, double-blind trial in 153 children aged 1 to 18 with acute cold symptoms who used the spray or a salt-water spray for 7 days, the treatment was described as safe and well tolerated, with fewer side effects observed with carrageenan than with placebo; the abstract does not say what the side effects were. In a randomised crossover trial in 42 adults with grass pollen allergy, a carrageenan-containing nasal spray had a similar incidence of adverse events to a comparator spray and no treatment. A 2021 systematic review of four placebo-controlled trials of the spray for colds describes a favourable safety profile but gives no event counts. The abstracts of a 211-adult cold trial and a 394-person trial in hospital staff caring for COVID-19 patients give no adverse-event data, and an 8-week prevention study in 102 adults reports low compliance with daily use. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
